analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA limits on power plant carbon emissions until several agencies certify no job, economic, or rate increases would result.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred EPA carbon limits on power plants until four agencies certified zero job or cost impacts, died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred the EPA from limiting carbon dioxide emissions from any power plant — new or existing — until four different offices certified in advance that the rule would cause no job losses, no drop in GDP, no increase in electricity rates, and no threat to electric reliability. Those certifications were effectively impossible to give, so the bill would have shut down federal carbon regulation of power plants. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be coal producers and coal-fired power plants, which would have been shielded from any new EPA limits on their carbon emissions. Coal-mining communities dependent on those jobs would have gained protection from regulation-driven job losses. Electricity customers might have avoided some compliance costs passed through in rates in the short term.

how_it_helps.text: For coal-mining communities and coal-dependent regions, the bill would have required the Secretary of Labor to certify that any new carbon rule causes no job loss, directly addressing the employment threat regulators were seen as posing [S2] [S3].
It would have required the Energy Information Administration to certify that no rule could raise electricity rates, a protection framed for household and business ratepayers [S2] [S3].
For utilities and power plant operators, it would have removed the threat of EPA carbon limits on both new and existing plants, giving the entire fossil-fuel fleet regulatory certainty [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on the public at large: the bill would have blocked any federal limit on power-plant carbon pollution unless four separate agencies certified there would be no job loss, no GDP loss, no electricity rate increase, and no reliability impact — effectively preventing the rules from ever taking effect, since predicting zero cost with certainty is not possible. Americans would bear the consequences of unchecked carbon emissions from power plants.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via unaddressed climate harm

drawbacks.text: The certification requirements were effectively impossible to satisfy: no agency can honestly certify in advance that a regulation will cause literally zero job losses, zero GDP loss, and zero rate increases, so the bill would have functioned as a permanent prohibition on regulating power-plant carbon emissions [S3].

The bill would have left the health and climate costs of power-plant carbon pollution — including extreme weather, air quality impacts, and the long-run risks of climate change — entirely unaddressed and unpriced [S2] [S3].

Supporters' job-protection framing applies mainly to a concentrated coal workforce; the same regulation-blocked approach offers no transition assistance or alternative plan for those workers if coal employment declines for market reasons [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, near-term protection to a specific group — coal workers and coal-dependent regions facing job losses from carbon rules — and short-term relief to ratepayers. But its mechanism was not a balanced weighing of costs and benefits: requiring four agencies to certify zero job loss, zero GDP loss, and zero rate increases is a standard no regulation could meet, so the bill was structured to end carbon regulation of power plants outright rather than to moderate it. The costs it prevented utilities from bearing would not have disappeared; they would have been shifted to the public as unaddressed climate and air-quality damage. On balance, the benefits were concentrated and the costs diffuse and larger.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without any hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell introduced the bill on June 3, 2014, joined by six original cosponsors and 13 total Republican cosponsors
The bill was read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee the same day
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The coal industry is better off because the bill died without becoming law would be backwards — in fact, because the bill failed, EPA authority to regulate power-plant carbon emissions was left intact, which is the outcome favored by groups supporting climate action. The coal industry lost its attempt to legislate a shield from carbon rules in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal industry; climate rules stayed in place

for.name: Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up 13 Republican cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred on June 3, 2014; no hearings, markup, or vote ever occurred

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never took it up.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose was to prevent any EPA limit on carbon emissions from power plants, which are the main market for coal. Blocking the rules would have preserved coal plants' revenue at the cost of leaving their carbon pollution unregulated.

Fossil-fueled utilities would have avoided compliance costs for new and existing plants. Ordinary customers might see lower rates in the near term, but the bill would shift the larger costs of carbon pollution onto the public.

By blocking carbon regulation of fossil plants, the bill would have removed the main policy driver pushing electricity generation toward renewables, delaying investment in wind, solar, and related industries.
